author: blu
body: It is PURE: records in, records out, no socket and no clock. A whole authenticated handshake between a client and a server runs as an ordinary battery sample by shuttling the emitted records between two endpoints, exactly the way the DTLS loopback shuttles datagrams.

author: blu
body: A client carries its X25519 private key, a 32-byte handshake random, the trust anchors it will accept, the calendar time (14 ASCII digits) it checks certificate validity against, and THE NAME IT DIALLED. Entropy and clock enter from the caller and are never invented here.

author: blu
body: The name is a parameter and not a setter, and that is the whole point of this signature. It used to be optional -- `tls-ep-expect-peer` set it after the fact, an unset name meant "anything matches", and every caller in the tree left it unset, so a certificate from any trusted authority authenticated for every host. An optional security check that defaults to permissive is not a check; it is a place where one could have gone. Made required, the type checker visits every caller and asks the question.

author: blu
body: A server presents a certificate chain (leaf first) and the Ed25519 private key that matches the leaf, and signs the transcript with it.

author: blu
body: The Certificate message: parse the chain, walk it to an anchor at the client's calendar time, and check the leaf's subject against the pinned peer if one is set. On success keep the leaf's key.

author: blu
body: The whole server flight in one place: ServerHello in the clear, then EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished each in its own record under the server handshake key. The application secrets are derived over the transcript through the server Finished -- the same hash the client's Finished will be checked against.
